articles.title: Embattled Spanish PM Sánchez insists no prior warnings before Ceuta crisis
articles.summary: Spain's prime minister tells parliament it is absurd to think the government knew and did nothing, after thousands join protests in Spanish cities.
articles.body:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said no-one foresaw the influx of 72,000 migrants in the exclave of Ceuta, as pressure mounts over his handling of the crisis.

"It's absurd to think that the government knew and did nothing," Sánchez told Spain's parliament on Thursday, hours after tens of thousands of people joined protests across the country backed by opposition parties.

Sánchez also maintained there was no evidence Morocco was behind the mass crossing and there had been "close co-ordination" between the two countries.

A Spanish police report has highlighted the "total permissiveness" of Moroccan security forces, although senior officials insist it does not point the finger at Rabat.

Although most of the migrants have been sent back to Morocco, some 5,000 remain on the streets and beaches of Ceuta, on the North African coast, including as many as 1,400 children.

There have been several reports that Spanish officials had been warned of a rise in sea arrivals over the border at Ceuta, following a Spanish court ruling that many migrants misunderstood to mean they would not be pushed back if they swam across.

Opposition People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo accused the government of lying and a cover-up, and said the prime minister should resign.

Spain's handling of the migrant influx angered some of its European partners, and Italy responded by imposing border restrictions on arrivals from Spain.

The large turnout for the demonstrations in Madrid and other cities on Wednesday underlined the pressure Sánchez is under domestically too.

The protests were ostensibly held to express support for the people of Ceuta, but as frequent anti-government chants have shown, they also reflected public anger at the ongoing crisis.

As Thursday's fierce debate in Congress showed, the situation in Ceuta has developed from a humanitarian and logistical crisis into a major political challenge for the Socialist leader.

One of the issues Sánchez is having to explain is his government's bilateral relationship with Morocco.

He has tried to walk a delicate line between defending his refusal to blame Morocco while reprimanding it for the sovereignty claims it has been making in recent weeks on both Ceuta and its fellow Spanish exclave of Melilla.

Sánchez has been careful until now not to criticise Rabat and he said he would stick to "proven, verified facts", although he did complain of "unacceptable" statements by two Moroccan ministers about Ceuta and its sister city Melilla.

Moroccan Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi has spoken of his country's "historical and geographical right" to the cities and proposed talks with Spain on the issue.

The two cities have the EU's only land borders in North Africa and Sánchez told parliament: "Ceuta is not the border of Spain, it is Spain on the border [of Europe]."

Protests in Spain against government's handling of Ceuta migrant crisis

Sexual assaults happening almost every day in Ceuta, prosecutors say

Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues

Politicians to both his left and right point to what they say is Morocco's track record of using the border with Spain as leverage when it has a grievance.

Many have interpreted the police report pointing to the role of Moroccan security forces in the July crossing as reinforcing this theory, although Sánchez maintained there was no solid evidence of government involvement.

The report, commissioned by a High Court judge, said security forces had "made no serious attempt" to stop the influx and quoted some migrants saying Moroccan gendarmes had even provided guidance.

Responding to the revelations, as well as media reports before the influx, Feijóo told MPs that the crisis had "originated in Morocco, was consented to by Morocco and there are indications that Morocco co-ordinated it and the government knew because it had been warned about it".

Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.

Sánchez said King Felipe VI would visit Ceuta and Melilla in the coming weeks to convey Spain's commitment to the two cities, although officials say no date has been set.

He praised the response of Ceuta police who had chosen to "defend human life" when the influx took place, rather than defend the border. He also highlighted close co-operation with Moroccan authorities over the return of more than 90% of the migrants in the following 72 hours.

He addressed the "difficult times" faced by the residents of Ceuta, as he explained the "complexity" of what had happened on 30 and 31 July.

He spoke of an "episode in which numerous actors and interests converge", doubling down on his assertion that hoaxes and rumours spread by social media had sparked the crisis.

He has already blamed trafficking gangs and angered Russia and Israel for highlighting social media linked to both countries along with "an international far-right movement". He told MPs that there was no evidence of state actors being involved but doubled down on his allegations of accounts linked to the two countries.

Ceuta was "a humanitarian crisis and also an administrative challenge within the city itself", he added.

articles.title: In 2007, American Peace Corps volunteer Laura Kutner began collecting plastic bottles in Granados; by 2009, they formed 2 schoolrooms and inspired 10 more schools
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Laura Kutner, a Peace Corps volunteer, repurposed 8,000 plastic bottles to create schoolrooms in Granados, Guatemala, inspiring a movement in sustainable construction and waste management across multiple communities.
articles.body: A discarded plastic bottle is usually treated as a piece of waste, but in Granados, Guatemala, thousands of them became part of a school. When American Peace Corps volunteer Laura Kutner arrived in the mountainous community in 2007, she encountered both a shortage of classroom space and a persistent waste problem. Two unfinished classrooms already had metal frames and roofs, but there was not enough money to complete the walls. Kutner eventually found a way to turn the rubbish around the community into a construction material.From litter to building materialAccording to Smithsonian Magazine, Granados, in Guatemala's Baja Verapaz region, had limited waste-disposal options, and rubbish frequently accumulated around the community. Kutner noticed the problem while working with local students and began considering whether some of that waste could be put to practical use. The idea came while she was sitting with students and drinking from a plastic bottle. She realised that the bottle was roughly the same width as the metal framing of the unfinished classrooms. Kutner had also encountered examples from elsewhere in Latin America where plastic bottles packed with waste were being used as building blocks. With the support of local engineers, she began adapting the approach for the school. The process was simple, but labour-intensive. Students and residents collected discarded plastic bottles, cleaned them and packed them tightly with inorganic waste such as plastic bags, wrappers and aluminium packaging. Paper and cardboard were excluded because they could decompose inside the bottles. The resulting "eco-bricks" were then placed inside metal frames and enclosed with chicken wire before the walls were covered with concrete.Kutner and school principal Reyna Ortiz organised workshops to explain how the bottles had to be prepared. Students were encouraged to collect and fill bottles themselves, and as the project required more material, volunteers also travelled to neighbouring communities to collect additional bottles and waste. What began as a way to complete two unfinished classrooms consequently expanded into a broader community clean-up effort. Construction of the walls began in February 2009. Kutner was later transferred to San Miguel Dueñas, but continued travelling back to Granados as the project neared completion. By October that year, the wall was finished, forming part of the two-room school.What the bottles could actually doThe Granados project was more than an unusual recycling exercise. It demonstrated how a material with little immediate value could be incorporated into a low-cost construction system when conventional building materials were difficult to afford. Research published in Materials & Design later examined the physical properties of PET bottle eco-bricks made by packing waste plastic into bottles. Laboratory tests found that their mechanical strength was closely related to how heavily the bottles were packed, while the researchers also identified potential benefits in sound insulation and light transmission. The study concluded that such eco-bricks could have construction applications, although their suitability depends on how they are manufactured and where they are used. This is important because a plastic bottle does not automatically become a replacement for a concrete block simply because it is tightly packed with rubbish.An idea that travelled beyond GranadosThe most lasting part of the project was perhaps what happened after the classrooms were completed. Kutner continued sharing the construction method, while other volunteers and communities became interested in the approach. Smithsonian reported that 10 additional schools had been built in Guatemala using the plastic-bottle technique. The Peace Corps also documented how the project encouraged communities to think differently about waste. Instead of treating discarded bottles and wrappers solely as rubbish, residents could collect, sort and repurpose some of that material. The project therefore connected two local problems, unfinished school construction and unmanaged waste, through a single community effort.According to a field report published in Children, Youth and Environments, Laura Kutner’s classroom project in Granados, Guatemala, involved children and young people in every stage, from collecting waste to constructing the classrooms. She highlighted hands-on learning, teamwork, creativity and community participation as key to creating more sustainable projects. The Granados classrooms were completed in 2009 and are now about 17 years old. However, the available reports do not provide a recent assessment of their condition or long-term performance.The project showed something more practical: even a material regarded as worthless can become useful when a community has the need, organisation and technical guidance to put it to another purpose. In Granados, thousands of bottles that might otherwise have remained scattered around the town instead became part of a school where children could learn. And the method did not remain confined to those two classrooms. It became an example that other communities in Guatemala chose to adapt, turning a small local experiment into a much wider idea.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.Social media also played a role in encouraging the crossings.According to the BBC, numerous posts circulated in August portraying the border fence between Morocco and Ceuta as safe and easy to cross, despite at several dying while attempting to swim around the border fence, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.Morocco has long claimed Ceuta, along with the neighbouring Spanish autonomous city of Melilla. articles.title: In the 1930s, Canada planted white spruce across native prairie; decades after the trees were removed, scientists found the ecosystem still hadn't recovered
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In the 1930s, white spruce plantations were established on native prairie in what is now known as the ‘Riding Mountain National Park’ in Manitoba. Dec.
articles.body: In the 1930s, white spruce plantations were established on native prairie in what is now known as the ‘Riding Mountain National Park’ in Manitoba. Decades later, the plantations were removed in an effort to restore the original northern fescue prairie. But according to a study titled ‘Legacy effects of afforestation on prairie plant and seed bank communities in a northern Canadian prairie,’ taking away the trees did not simply return the ecosystem to its former state. The researchers found that the effects of the plantations continued to shape both the plants above ground and the tiny organisms living in the soil long after tree removal. The findings show how a landscape may begin to look like its old self while important changes remain hidden below the surface. The study offers a long-term warning that restoring native prairie after decades of tree cover may require far more than simply cutting the trees down.Why Canada’s native prairie hadn’t recovered after removing the white spruce treesThe study examined two historic white spruce plantations that had been established between 1930 and 1940 on rough fescue prairie in Riding Mountain National Park. The researchers compared three different parts of these landscapes which includes native prairie that had never been planted with trees, areas where the white spruce plantation remained, and sites where the trees had been removed at different times. This approach allowed the scientists to look beyond the immediate effects of tree removal and ask a more difficult question as to ‘what happens to a prairie when more time passes after restoration begins.’According to the study, planting trees had changed the prairie ecosystem above and below ground. Even after the spruce had been removed, the restored areas did not simply follow a straightforward path back to the conditions found in untouched native prairie. The researchers focused on plant communities as well as soil nematodes (tiny roundworms that occupy different positions in the soil food web). These organisms can reveal changes that are not always visible in the plants growing above ground.Decades of tree cover left lasting changes beneath the soilThe study found that changes in plant communities after tree removal were accompanied by changes in soil nematodes. As the restored sites aged, the balance between different nematode feeding groups also shifted. Nematodes that feed on fungi and bacteria declined over time, while plant-parasitic nematodes became more common and reached levels similar to those recorded in native prairie. This suggested that some parts of the soil ecosystem were changing in the direction of the original grassland. However, recovery was not complete. The study found that the overall diversity of both plant and nematode communities declined over time and was lowest in the oldest restored treatment. That was a striking result because it suggested that simply allowing more years to pass after tree removal did not necessarily lead to a closer match with the native prairie. In other words, restoration was not a straight line from plantation to fully recovered grassland.Could the prairie ever return to its original stateThe findings challenge the idea that removing an ecological disturbance automatically reverses its effects. The white spruce trees were gone from the restored sites, but decades of tree growth had left behind a legacy that continued to influence the ecosystem. A prairie is not defined only by the plants above the surface. Its roots, soil organisms and food webs are also important parts of the ecosystem. When trees replace native grassland for many decades, those relationships can change in ways that are difficult to reverse. The study's results show why restoration projects cannot always be judged by appearance alone. An area may once again contain prairie vegetation while its underground community remains different from that of an undisturbed grassland. The researchers therefore highlighted soil nematodes as useful indicators of restoration. Because these organisms responded to changes in plant communities and the passage of time after tree removal, they provided another way of measuring how the ecosystem was changing.The oldest restored sites still showed signs of ecological changePerhaps the most important message from the study is that time alone does not guarantee ecological recovery. The oldest restored sites did not have the highest overall diversity. Instead, both plant and nematode diversity were lowest there. This does not mean that every part of the ecosystem was moving further away from prairie conditions. These mixed results showed that recovery can occur differently across an ecosystem. One part may begin to resemble the original habitat while another remains altered. That makes long-term monitoring especially important. A restoration project may appear successful shortly after an intervention, yet its ecological direction can change as years pass.Lesson from Canada's altered prairie landscapeHuman decisions can leave ecological effects that persist far longer than the original activity itself. In this case, trees planted on native prairie in the 1930s were eventually removed, yet the prairie had not simply returned to its previous ecological condition. The research showed that the legacy of afforestation remained visible in the structure and diversity of plant and soil communities. The study does not suggest that restoration is pointless. Instead, it reveals how complex the process can be. Removing an obvious pressure is often only the beginning of ecological recovery. For prairie conservation, the findings underline the importance of protecting native ecosystems before major changes occur. Decades after the first white spruce trees were planted, and years after many of them were removed, the prairie was still carrying the ecological memory of what had happened.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Kirstie Allsopp airlifted to hospital after fall during birthday celebrations
articles.summary: The TV presenter slipped and injured her leg while walking home from a beach in Devon with her family.
articles.body:
TV presenter Kirstie Allsopp has revealed she was airlifted to hospital for surgery after slipping and injuring her leg while walking home from a beach in Devon on holiday.

The Location, Location, Location host, 55, shared a photo on Instagram of her lying in an ambulance with cuts on her face and a breathing tube up her nose.

She explained in the adjoining caption how she had "slipped on a muddy patch on the steep path", while walking back with her family following her birthday celebrations.

"We have a picnic on the beach at Welcombe Mouth, a swim and a walk back to the house for some cake," she wrote of the longstanding family tradition.

It took "a whole host of people to get me to hospital", she added.

"After a little wait while poor Oscar [her son, 18] ran as fast as he could to get help, and the RNLI Bude Lifeboat paramedics and Cornwall Air Ambulance tracked me down."

She then asked for help identifying those who had helped her, noting how she had been given "a huge amount of painkillers" so was "high as a kite!"

"Everyone at Barnstaple hospital has been amazing, kind and caring, so many lovely people doing their absolute best."

Allsopp is known for presenting the long-running Channel 4 property programme alongside Phil Spencer.

She confirmed she had undergone an operation on her leg - sharing pictures of her leg in bandages along with an X-ray - but would be "home soon".

"It'll be a boot and crutches for a while, but I feel very, very lucky that it was possible to reach me and get me to hospital so quickly, and I have a job that I can do on crutches," she continued.

"Not a birthday I am going to forget in a hurry and again, thank you to all those who have been involved in my care."

In the comments section of her Instagram post, fellow broadcaster and musician Jools Holland said: "Poor you get well soon."

Property developer and husband of Princess Beatrice, Edoardo Mapelli Mozzi, added: "Wishing you a speedy recovery."

Interior designer Rita Konig commented: "I have to say, I thought about this on my way down some steep paths to the beach this summer and wondered what the exit strategy is if one slips and busts something like an ankle!! Sending lots of love."

articles.title: Most exclusive Country Club that invited Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sanchez as special guests for at an event, but will still give them its membership
articles.summary: Tech News News: Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos were invited as special guests to an event at one of America's most exclusive country clubs. Six months later, how.
articles.body: Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos were invited as special guests to an event at one of America's most exclusive country clubs. Six months later, however, the Amazon founder still has not been given membership. Jeff Bezos attended Indian Creek Country Club's annual dock party in February this year, meeting members and making the case for joining the club. But at this private club in Miami's Indian Creek island, being one of the world's richest people—or even owning multiple homes on the island—is not enough to secure a place on its membership list.Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez attended club event as ‘special guests’'The couple attended the Indian Creek Country Club's annual dock party in February as special guests, where members gathered for a social event. According to people who attended, Jeff Bezos spent time speaking with club members and introducing himself to guests.The visit was significant because Bezos was not simply attending as another island resident. He was hoping to win over members who would ultimately decide whether he could join the club. Yet the invitation to attend the event came with no promise of membership. Six months later, Bezos had still not received an invitation to join, according to people familiar with the matter.Jeff Bezos owns three properties on the island, but that doesn't guarantee membershipJeff Bezos has acquired three properties on Indian Creek island for a combined price of about $234 million, according to public records. The island is home to billionaires and business leaders and is often referred to as the “Billionaire Bunker.”But Indian Creek Country Club operates differently from many residential communities. Buying a home on the island does not automatically make someone a club member. At the same time, people who do not live on the island can also apply to join. That means Bezos can own multiple properties on Indian Creek and still need approval from the club's existing members before he can play on its golf course as a member.Why joining the country club is not just about moneyFounded in 1929, Indian Creek Country Club has around 350 members, and joining requires more than paying the fees. The club reportedly charges an initiation fee close to $1 million, along with annual dues of about $44,000.Applicants usually need sponsorship from two current members and recommendation letters from five others. They are also expected to attend events and get to know existing members. A six-member membership committee considers nominees before the club's 15-member board makes the final decision.Other famous residents are also outside the clubNotably, Jeff Bezos is not the only high-profile person living on Indian Creek who is not a member. The report says other wealthy residents, including Mark Zuckerberg, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, are also not members. Some applicants have faced years of waiting. Kushner and Trump, for example, have worked to build relationships within the community after reportedly facing an initial setback in their efforts to join.Other well-known applicants have had different experiences. Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon ultimately became a member after facing opposition, according to people connected to the club.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Norway seizes Russian ship in Arctic over Crimea compensation claim
articles.summary: Moscow challenges Norway’s seizure of vessel, the Professor Molchanov, calling it an act of piracy.
articles.body:
Norway has seized a Russian ship in ⁠the Arctic to ⁠enforce a compensation claim by Ukrainian energy firm Naftogaz, linked to Russian asset seizures in Crimea.

Norway seized the ship on Wednesday, after Moscow failed to pay Naftogaz $4.22bn plus interest and legal costs to compensate for ⁠assets it seized in ⁠Crimea after a tribunal ruling at The Hague in 2023.

In a post on X, Naftogaz said the seizure made up “part of global efforts to enforce the arbitral award obtained by Naftogaz against the Russian Federation in connection with the unlawful expropriation of their assets in Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014”.

The vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was taken off the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard after a 24-hour standoff with the Norwegian Coast Guard, according ⁠to Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz.⁠

Russian state news agency TASS quoted a Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson as calling the Norwegian action “piracy”.

Alexei Chekunkov, Russia’s ⁠minister for the development of the Russian ⁠Far East and Arctic, ⁠said Moscow would challenge the ruling.

Chekunkov called Norway’s seizure of the Professor Molchanov “another ‌example of Western countries’ legal nihilism and lawlessness,” according to the ‌Interfax ‌news agency.

Naftogaz has been pursuing legal action against Russia since 2016 to seek compensation for the expropriation of its property in Crimea.

“Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award,” said Naftogaz Acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko.

“We will continue to pursue Russian assets around the world until the compensation ‌awarded ‌to Naftogaz and other Naftogaz Group companies is paid,” the Ukrainian company said.

Covington, the law firm, said it had been tracking the Professor Molchanov, a Russian-owned vessel that is used for commercial cruises, for months.

The ship was being used for commercial expedition cruises, including to Svalbard, according to the company.

Naftogaz said the passengers on board are being handled by Norwegian authorities.

articles.title: EU foreign ministers fail to break deadlock over Israel and Ukraine
articles.summary: EU officials met in Ireland but failed to agree on imposing trade sanctions on Israel or military support for Ukraine.
articles.body:
Wicklow, Ireland – “We have reached an impasse,” said Ireland’s Foreign Minister Helen McEntee at a gathering of European Union officials on Tuesday, summing up the bloc’s increasingly fractured position on trade sanctions on Israel.

Ireland, which currently holds the European Council’s presidency, and Spain pushed for EU-wide trade curbs on goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank at the September 1-2 meeting in Wicklow amid escalating settler violence against Palestinians.

France pressed for a stronger European response to Israeli rhetoric against Palestinians. “Condemnations from Israeli officials have been a good start, but they are not enough,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told reporters, referring to Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s call for mass displacement in the Gaza Strip.

But several EU nations, including Germany and Hungary, opposed the move during the two-day informal gathering.

The Gymnich meeting, as the gathering is called, opened on Tuesday with renewed efforts by Dublin to revive discussions on sanctions against Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank – a proposal that has largely stalled in recent months because of divisions among member states.

The EU is Israel’s largest trading partner, with bilateral trade standing at more than $50bn.

Kaja Kallas, the EU’s foreign policy chief, acknowledged that the absence of unanimity had once again prevented the bloc from moving forward on measures against Israel, despite growing pressure from several governments for a stronger European response to illegal settlement expansion and settler violence in the occupied Palestinian territory.

Ireland has argued that the EU’s credibility depends on applying international law consistently, regardless of the conflict under discussion. Dublin has also pointed to what it sees as a disparity between the bloc’s willingness to impose sanctions and other measures in response to Russia’s actions in Ukraine and its reluctance to take comparable action against Israel despite its ongoing genocide in Gaza and alarming rate of violence in the occupied Palestinian territory.

The disagreement is not simply over how member states view the Israel-Palestinian conflict, but over what practical steps the EU should take. Ireland and several other governments have pushed for stronger measures, including action against individuals involved in settler violence and restrictions on trade linked to illegal Israeli settlements, while other member states have been reluctant to support such proposals.

Ukraine dominated much of the first day’s talks, with Kyiv continuing to call for greater European military support.

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has entered its fifth year, with Moscow escalating drone and missile attacks against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.

Kyiv again urged European governments to provide additional air defence systems after months of sustained Russian drone attacks.

Yet ministers again failed to bridge their differences.

Greece and Spain maintained their opposition to using common EU funds to finance further purchases of air defence systems, leaving Ukraine without the additional missiles and interceptors it had hoped for from the meeting.

On the sidelines of the talks, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha appealed directly to European media, warning that delays in military support would come at a growing cost as Russia has intensified its aerial campaign. It did not seem to move the needle much.

The Ukraine debate also exposed another longstanding fault line within the bloc.

While Poland, Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands renewed calls to use frozen Russian sovereign assets to finance Ukraine’s military effort, Belgium, which holds the largest share of those assets, again resisted the proposal, citing unresolved legal and financial concerns.

Meanwhile, ministers also turned their attention to the wider Middle East.

The US-Israel war on Iran, now in its seventh month, has left European governments with limited diplomatic leverage despite the conflict directly affecting the continent, including concerns over energy security for the upcoming winter months.

The future of Lebanon, which continued to be attacked by Israel, was also discussed, with ministers considering a possible EU mission to train the Lebanese army as the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) ends this year.

Elsewhere, on August 30, EU forces operating in the Mediterranean boarded a tanker suspected of being linked to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, as part of broader European efforts to enforce sanctions against Moscow and disrupt attempts to evade them.

And if the external crises were not enough, the ministers also had some internal fires to deal with.

Just a day before the meeting, Italy renewed enhanced air and land checks on travellers arriving from Spain following a dispute linked to migration and border controls. Madrid responded by extending reciprocal measures.

The dispute followed an influx of migrants in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta, after which Italy introduced additional checks on some travellers from Spain.

Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares urged other member states to support Madrid’s position on the border measures while criticising governments that, he said, had failed to support Spain during the Ceuta crisis.

At the end of the two-day meeting on Wednesday, ministers left having said more or less what they had said before.

“We are a dog that barks but doesn’t bite,” Luxembourg’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Xavier Bettel said at the meeting, expressing his frustration at the lack of support to sanction Israel.

After the meeting, the bloc is more or less where it started – plenty of shared concern, but very little shared action. The unanimity rule remains the EU’s Achilles heel – everyone has to agree, which means, in practice, almost nothing gets done.

articles.title: Former California mayor sentenced to prison for sexually abusing 17-year-old foreign exchange student
articles.summary: US News: Robert Brian Bassett, a former mayor in California, sentenced to 4 years for sexually abusing a 17-year-old foreign exchange student. Victim's testimony highlights betrayal and grooming. Bassett faces sex offender registration upon release.
articles.body: A former California mayor has been sentenced to four years and four months in prison after admitting to sexually abusing a 17-year-old foreign exchange student who had been staying at his home.Robert Brian Bassett, 58, was sentenced on Wednesday after pleading no contest to three felony child-sex-abuse charges, The New York Times reported.The teenager had been living with Bassett and his family in Biggs, Northern California, from April to November 2023 while taking part in a foreign exchange programme. Prosecutors said Bassett spent months grooming her before sexually abusing her multiple times.Prosecutors argued that Bassett’s position as her host and his role as mayor made the abuse a serious breach of trust. They cited the girl’s vulnerability, the grooming and the abuse of the trust placed in him as factors warranting the maximum sentence.The victim told the court that she continues to deal with the consequences of the abuse, including the betrayal by someone she had trusted while living far from her family.The investigation began after police arrested Bassett on July 9 and searched his Biggs home. Investigators later contacted the victim in her home country, where she disclosed what had happened.Bassett served on the Biggs City Council and was mayor from 2022 to December 2024.He stayed on the council after leaving the mayor's office but resigned in early 2025 amid an earlier extortion investigation.A separate criminal investigation into his conduct while mayor eventually resulted in the plea agreement. Two additional felony charges were dismissed as part of the deal.Bassett will have to register as a sex offender for 10 years after completing his prison sentence.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In Italy, some restaurants let diners take their plates home: The 60-year tradition that turned plates into souvenirs
articles.summary: Europe News: Imagine finishing a meal at an Italian restaurant and leaving with the plate on which your food was served. It sounds unusual, but for more than six d.
articles.body: Imagine finishing a meal at an Italian restaurant and leaving with the plate on which your food was served. It sounds unusual, but for more than six decades, a group of Italian restaurants has turned this simple piece of tableware into a lasting souvenir. Known as the Piatti del Buon Ricordo, or “Plates of Good Memory”, the tradition began in 1964 with an idea to promote Italy's regional cuisine and encourage diners to discover local specialities. Participating restaurants offer specially designed ceramic plates featuring images linked to their signature dishes, restaurants or surrounding areas. Diners who order the designated speciality can take the commemorative plate home, creating a physical reminder of their meal and journey. More than 60 years after the tradition began, the practice continues across Italy and beyond.How Italy turned restaurant plates into souvenirsThe story began in 1964, when advertising executive and cultural promoter Dino Villani helped establish the Unione Ristoranti del Buon Ricordo. Twelve restaurants came together in Milan in April that year to promote an idea centred on Italy's regional cooking. At the time, traditional regional cuisine was competing for attention with French-influenced cooking, and Villani wanted to encourage greater appreciation of the dishes and culinary identities found across Italy. The organisation created an unusual way of connecting food with memory. Participating restaurants would offer a distinctive local speciality and provide diners with a ceramic plate designed to commemorate that dish and the place where it was served. The concept transformed a restaurant meal into something that could be remembered long after the diner had left.The plates associated with Buon Ricordo are not simply the ordinary dinner plates used by restaurants. They are specially designed commemorative ceramics produced for the programme. Each participating restaurant has its own plate, generally featuring an illustration connected with its signature speciality, local ingredients, town or surrounding area. The name Buon Ricordo translates roughly as “good memory”, reflecting the purpose behind the objects. Instead of leaving diners with only the memory of a meal, the tradition gives them something physical to take home and display. The plate therefore represents both the food they ate and the place where they experienced it.Why diners can take the plates homeThe souvenir is tied to the restaurant's designated Buon Ricordo speciality or menu. A diner who orders the relevant offering receives the commemorative plate as part of the tradition. This is why it would be misleading to suggest that customers at these restaurants can simply remove any plate from the table after eating. The programme specifically involves plates created as souvenirs for participating restaurants. The unusual arrangement was designed to strengthen the connection between a regional dish and the memory of visiting the restaurant where it was served.Each plate represents a different place and dishOne of the most distinctive features of the collection is that every restaurant's plate can tell a different story. The artwork may show the restaurant's signature dish, an ingredient associated with the speciality or an image connected with the local area. This creates a visual link between cuisine and geography. A diner collecting plates from different restaurants can therefore build a record of regional Italian food through the designs on the ceramics. The plate is not just a souvenir carrying a restaurant name. It is intended to represent the culinary identity of the place and the speciality that the restaurant has chosen to promote.The tradition quickly became a collecting hobbyThe idea grew rapidly after its launch. The original 12 restaurants had more than doubled by the end of the 1960s, while membership approached 100 by the end of the 1970s. In 1977, a separate Association of Collectors was established, reflecting the growing interest in the plates themselves. Travellers could visit participating restaurants, sample their regional specialities and take home the corresponding ceramic. Over time, collections became a way of documenting journeys through Italy, with each plate serving as a physical reminder of a particular restaurant, dish and destination.The plates are hand-painted in ItalyThe ceramics have traditionally been produced in Vietri sul Mare on the Amalfi Coast, an area with a long-established reputation for ceramics. The Buon Ricordo organisation says the plates are made using clay associated with the area and are hand-painted by artisans. This craftsmanship gives the souvenirs a character that distinguishes them from ordinary mass-produced tourist merchandise. Each restaurant's design is created specifically around its food and local identity, meaning the finished plate becomes a small piece of culinary and artistic representation of that place.Graphic designer Paolo Argenton has designed the Buon Ricordo plates since 1985. His role has been to translate each restaurant's speciality and territory into a distinctive ceramic design. Restaurants identify the dish they want to represent, while the artwork can incorporate other visual references to the surrounding area. The result is a collection in which the plates share the same broad tradition but retain individual identities. This consistency combined with variety has helped make the ceramics recognisable as part of the Buon Ricordo tradition while giving collectors a reason to seek out plates from different restaurants.The idea was about protecting regional cuisineThe plates were never intended to be merely decorative souvenirs. Villani's wider goal was to promote Italy's regional culinary traditions and encourage diners to explore foods associated with different territories. The restaurant network provided a way to connect individual dishes with their local origins, while the plate gave diners a physical reminder of that experience. In this sense, the tradition became a form of culinary promotion and cultural preservation. Each restaurant was expected to have a strong connection with its territory and its designated speciality, reinforcing the idea that Italian cuisine is made up of many distinct regional traditions rather than one uniform national menu.The tradition spread beyond ItalyThe Buon Ricordo idea eventually crossed Italy's borders. According to the organisation's official history, the movement began expanding internationally during the 1980s. Restaurants outside Italy subsequently joined the network, allowing the tradition of regional Italian cuisine and commemorative plates to continue in other countries. The international restaurants became part of the same broader effort to promote Italian food culture, while giving diners abroad an opportunity to participate in a tradition that originated in Milan more than six decades ago.As the tradition grew, the plates developed a life beyond the restaurants that issued them. Collectors began searching for older and rarer examples, and vintage Buon Ricordo ceramics can now be found through collectors, antique markets and other secondary sources. The dedicated collectors' association, which dates back to 1977, reflects the depth of this interest. For some collectors, the appeal lies in the artwork and craftsmanship, while for others the plates represent memories of meals and journeys through different parts of Italy. A collection can consequently function almost like a visual travel diary, with each plate representing a different stop.More than 60 years later, the tradition continuesThe tradition is still active rather than simply being a relic of Italy's culinary past. The organisation's 2026 guide lists 111 participating establishments, including 103 in Italy and eight abroad. The number has changed considerably over the decades, so older reports may give different totals, but the current guide provides the latest official figure. What began with 12 restaurants in 1964 has therefore survived for more than six decades and continues to connect restaurants, regional dishes and commemorative ceramics.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Yair Netanyahu, Israeli PM’s son, angers UK right over Falklands comment
articles.summary: Accusing the UK government of ‘hypocrisy’, Yair Netanyahu backs Argentina’s claims to the British-held Falkland Islands.
articles.body:
Comments by Yair Netanyahu, the son of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, backing Argentina’s claim to the British-controlled Falkland Islands have caused an unlikely row with Britain’s right wing – one of the United Kingdom’s last reliable pro-Israel groups.

The younger Netanyahu waded into the longrunning territorial dispute over the South Atlantic archipelago last week, writing on X in Spanish: “The Falkland Islands belong to Argentina.”

Britain and Argentina fought a war over the islands in 1982 and continue to dispute their sovereignty.

In follow-up posts, he said that Israel should support Argentina’s claim because the Argentinian government, under far-right President Javier Milei, is more friendly to Israel.

He accused the UK of “hypocrisy and hostility towards Israel with their recognition of ‘Palestine’”, as well as of perpetuating “antisemitism” and “blood libels”.

UK’s Restore Britain party clashes with Yair Netanyahu

His comments came days before United States President Donald Trump, also a close ally of Milei, said the US was reviewing its stance on the Falklands.

While Yair Netanyahu’s remarks appeared intended as a shot at the UK’s Labour government, which includes both centre-left and left-wing politicians, they have also angered right-wing British figures who are typically pro-Israel.

Rupert Lowe, head of the far-right Restore Britain party, responded directly to him on X, saying that the Falklands would “remain” British and that a UK government led by his party would “go to war if necessary to ensure it”.

“You have enough problems to be focusing on in Israel”, Lowe responded, while calling on the Israeli government to clarify its position on the Falklands.

According to YouGov, just 3 percent of people polled would vote for Restore if a general election were held tomorrow.

Sir Conor Burns, a former MP with Britain’s Conservative Party, called Yair Netanyahu’s comments “stupid” and warned they would be “damaging to Israel’s cause on the [British] right”.

Far-right British activist Tommy Robinson, formerly called Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, a vocal backer of Israel, shared a post on X calling British sovereignty over the Falklands a “true fact”, without mentioning the son of the Israeli premier.

Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer on security studies at King’s College London, said the remarks were the latest example of him causing “consternation amongst Israel’s self-declared friends in Europe.”

“Yair Netanyahu has antagonised the constituency in Britain most inclined to defend Israel,” Geist Pinfold told Al Jazeera.

While not an Israeli government official, Geist Pinfold said that he “is alleged to have far more de facto power behind the scenes thanks to Benjamin Netanyahu’s increasingly autocratic style of leadership”.

James Vaughan, lecturer in international history at Aberystwyth University, said that remarks could alienate some on the British right, though it is not a united bloc.

While Britain’s mainstream right-wing movements are generally pro-Israel, elements of Britain’s “extreme right” have historically been an “anti-Israeli force in British politics,” Vaughan told Al Jazeera, adding that there are signs of Restore Britain “reverting to older, anti-Semitic traditions”.

Last year, Restore Britain’s Lowe said of a camera that would film him, “In days gone by you’d call it a Jewish camera, but that would be politically incorrect. Because it’s so small.” He has also called for kosher – as well as halal – meat to be banned. He has rejected accusations of anti-Semitism.

No Israeli government official has publicly endorsed Yair Netanyahu’s position on the Falklands.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar has, however, previously invoked the islands while defending Israel’s illegal settlement policy in the occupied West Bank.

During a United Nations Security Council debate in February, Saar said that Israeli settlements in the West Bank were located “in the cradle of our own civilisation”, contrasting them with the Falklands.

“It is our country; it’s not 13,000 kilometres away from our country, like the Falkland Islands, ” said Saar, addressing then-British Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper. “The Argentinians call it the Malvinas Islands – a dispute you haven’t solved with Argentina until today.”

Vaughan pointed out that the Falklands have long been a “thorny issue in UK-Israel relations”, including in the early 1980s, due to Israeli arms sales to Argentina.

“The fact that the current Israeli government is once again ‘playing the Falklands card’ is of little consequence in and of itself and probably tells us more about the current state of friendly relations between Israel and Argentina than anything else,” Vaughan told Al Jazeera.

Israeli officials have brought up other territorial issues when responding to criticism over Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestinian land.

On July 31, as Spanish authorities faced a wave of people rushing into its territory of Ceuta over the Moroccan border, Israeli ambassador to the United Nations Danny Danon goaded Spain over its control of the African enclave.

“Maybe before it continues lecturing us, it’s time it explained to the world why it [Spain] still maintains colonial enclaves in Africa,” Danon wrote in a post on X.

Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has noted that Israel is carrying out a genocide in Gaza, and Madrid has imposed sweeping measures, including a total arms embargo , against Israel.

Like the UK and other European countries, Spain also recognises Palestinian statehood .

Despite traditionally strong ties, there are signs of tension between Israel and Britain under Labour, which took power in 2024.

Under former Labour Prime Minister Keir Starmer, the UK paused free-trade talks with Israel and suspended some arms export licences. The UK has also imposed sanctions on far-right Israeli cabinet members Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

The UK’s new leader, Andy Burnham, is currently weighing further measures relating to illegal Israeli settlements.

Israeli officials have derided the UK as relations deteriorate. Prime Minister Netanyahu recently referred to the UK as the “Islamic Republic of Britain ”.

Vaughan said that the re-emergence of the Falklands issue is “indicative of underlying UK-Israeli tensions that are obviously rooted more in fundamental disagreements about Gaza, the West Bank and wider Middle Eastern conflicts”.

articles.title: Gloria Steinem, fierce feminist trailblazer, dies age 92
articles.summary: Gloria Steinem, the indefatigable feminist and journalist whose activism revolutionized the personal and professional lives of women, has died.
articles.body: Gloria Steinem, the indefatigable feminist and journalist whose activism revolutionized the personal and professional lives of women, has died. She was 92. Steinem “passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her,” a post on her official Instagram page said Thursday. It added that she died Wednesday, although it did not give a cause of death. “Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” the post said. She “lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humor,” the statement added. It hailed her ability to welcome hundreds of guests into her living room for “Talking Circles” and was committed to using her home as a “center for social justice movements.” Her representatives asked her fans to light a candle in her honor and for donations to be made to her charity, Gloria’s Foundation. Steinem dedicated her life to causes ranging from reproductive freedom and domestic violence prevention to fighting workplace gender inequalities. She was the face of a movement that radically changed rights for women so they could eventually apply for credit cards without a man’s signature, be admitted to Ivy League schools that previously barred them, and legally get an abortion in the United States. A pioneer of the 1960s’ era of second-wave feminism, Steinem advocated for social issues, as well as wrote about them. Her first brush with national fame came in 1963, when she went undercover as a Playboy bunny and wrote an exposé about the poor working conditions that the servers in Hugh Hefner’s famed Playboy clubs endured. Steinem earned some of the highest recognitions possible, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s top civilian honor. But she came from humble beginnings — and had an unusual childhood. Born March 25, 1934, in Toledo, Ohio, Steinem and her older sister, Susanne, spent much of their early years crisscrossing the country with their parents, Leo and Ruth Steinem, who brought the family with him for his job as a traveling antiques salesman. Steinem did not attend school regularly until she was 11, after her parents divorced and she had moved back to Ohio with her mother. Ruth Steinem had mental health problems, something Steinem has said deeply influenced her. Seeing doctors dismiss her mother’s needs contributed to her desire to get women more of a voice in society. And being forced to care for her mother deterred her from wanting children of her own. “I’d already been the very small parent of a very big child — my mother,” she told People magazine in 1992. “I didn’t want to end up taking care of someone else.” In 1956, Steinem graduated from Smith College, the all-women’s liberal arts school in Massachusetts, with a degree in government — an uncommon major for women then. While overseas in London at age 22 after graduation, she discovered she was carrying an unwanted pregnancy. “I had all the usual fantasies — maybe if I go horseback riding, maybe if I throw myself down the stairs,” she recalled to NPR in 2021. Abortions were illegal at the time, but by “sheer luck,” she said, she found a physician who directed her to a doctor who was secretly doing abortions. She dedicated her 2015 memoir, “My Life on the Road,” to the doctor who referred her to the woman who performed her abortion. Steinem’s abortion spurred her lifelong interest in reproductive rights, but she did not publicly reveal that she had had it until 1969. In 2019, she told Al Jazeera it bothered her that the debate was framed as “pro-choice” versus “pro-life” and said no one is “pro” abortion. “Nobody would choose one if they didn’t have to,” she said. Steinem spent two years in India on a fellowship after she graduated college and later went to New York to pursue journalism, a field in which she struggled to be taken seriously as a woman. It wasn’t until her blockbuster piece on Playboy bunnies was published in 1963 in Show magazine that she gained recognition. For the two-part exposé, written in diary form, Steinem assumed a fake identity and accepted a job for several weeks as a bunny. The women, she wrote, were expected to always “think about something happy” so they could put on a cheerful persona for their male clientele, even as their clubs demanded exorbitant portions of their tips and forced them to dress in skimpy outfits and heels so high, Steinem’s feet became swollen and permanently expanded a half-size. In the following years, while growing her profile as a feminist activist, she helped launch two key magazines. In 1968, she became a founding editor and political columnist for New York magazine. Her 1969 article “After Black Power, Women’s Liberation” cemented her place as a feminist icon. 'Too pretty' and other criticisms In 1971, she co-founded Ms. magazine, which started as an insert in New York magazine before becoming its own standalone magazine the following year. In 1976, it became the first national publication to spotlight domestic violence on its cover. As Steinem established herself as a leader in the fight for legalizing abortion, for gender equality in the workplace, against child abuse and in other areas, she was not without controversy. Some, including those in her own movement, felt she was “too pretty” for the feminist message she was trying to convey and that the 1970s miniskirts she would sometimes wear for her television interviews were working against her. In 1992, she released a book entitled “Revolution From Within: A Book of Self-Esteem” that focused on personal development. The idea behind it, she explained, was that to effect change on a societal level, individuals need inner strength. But it was panned by some reviewers as a pivot away from activism instead. In September 2020, while Donald Trump was president, Steinem spoke about how she handled criticism. “The most painful criticism or attacks come from people who share your values, not people who don’t share your values,” she told The New York Times. “If Trump spoke well of me, I would shoot myself.” Steinem cared deeply about politics, co-founding the National Women’s Political Caucus in 1971 to increase the number of female legislators. Little slowed her down, including a diagnosis of breast cancer at age 52. She was diagnosed early and able to get it treated. She was 79 when then-President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Her life was depicted on screen multiple times, including in “Mrs. America,” an FX miniseries that streamed on Hulu in 2020. She received numerous accolades in journalism, including the Lifetime Achievement in Journalism Award from the Society of Professional Journalists. Steinem got married at age 66 to lawyer and entrepreneur David Bale, father of actor Christian Bale, in 2000. Many of her followers were surprised: Steinem had long dismissed marriage as an institution that ruined relationships. Bale died of lymphoma three years after they wed. When later asked why she changed her mind about marriage, she told a reporter, “I didn’t change. Marriage changed.” “If I had married when I was supposed to get married, I would have lost my name, my legal residence, my credit rating, many of my civil rights,” she added. “That’s not true anymore. It’s possible to make an equal marriage.” She told the Times that Bale helped her learn the importance of living in the moment and accomplishing what you set out to do. “Even if I live to 100, which I have every intention of doing, it’s not that long left,” she told the paper in 2020. “I just hope that I don’t die saying, ‘But! Wait!’”

articles.title: More than 80 migrants feared dead after boat rescued off Canary Islands
articles.summary: Rescuers found 44 survivors on board the vessel but bad weather meant they had to leave five bodies behind.
articles.body:
More than 80 people, including a baby, are feared to have died in a boat which was adrift in the Atlantic Ocean for 27 days.

Spanish Maritime Rescue teams located the vessel some 65 nautical miles southwest of Gran Canaria's coastal town of Arguineguín on Wednesday and found 44 survivors, with five dead bodies also on board.

The boat is believed to have departed The Gambia in West Africa in early August with 127 occupants on board. Human rights activist Helena Maleno Garzón, founder of Spanish charity Caminando Fronteras, said 83 people had lost their lives.

Rescuers were forced to leave the five bodies they found due to the rough sea conditions, Maritime Rescue said.

The organisation was unable to verify how many people were originally on board.

The 44 survivors are men from sub-Saharan Africa, Maritime Rescue said in a statement.

"Once the rescue was complete, adverse weather conditions in the area - featuring 20-knot winds and 2.5m waves - made it impossible to recover the five bodies found on board the vessel," it added.

Three of the survivors were airlifted to hospital in critical condition.

The rest were transported by sea to Gran Canaria, where they disembarked in the early hours of Thursday morning.

Fernando Clavijo, head of the Canary Islands government, posted on X: "It is intolerable that lives continue to be lost. The Canaries cannot get used to or accept as normal the fact that the Atlantic continues to be a death trap."

The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world's deadliest migration crossings.

Thousands of migrants attempt the perilous journey each year seeking to reach Spanish territory despite the risks posed by rough seas, strong currents and long distances.

articles.title: Gloria Steinem: Feminist activist and journalist dies, aged 92
articles.summary: Her foundation said she "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City, "surrounded by many who loved her".
articles.body:
Gloria Steinem, who became a face of the women's liberation movement in the US, has died, aged 92.

In a post on Instagram, her foundation said she "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City on Wednesday, "surrounded by many who loved her".

Steinem, who was a writer and magazine editor, co-founded the Women's Action Alliance - a group dedicated to fighting sexism - more than 50 years ago.

She started her career as a journalist in New York and went on to co-found Ms. magazine, one of the first publications to focus on women's issues other than housekeeping and beauty.

During the 1970s, Steinem was a vocal campaigner for women's reproductive rights, among other causes.

She herself obtained an illegal abortion in London when she was 22 years old, and years later celebrated the US Supreme Court's 1973 ruling in the case of Roe v Wade, which granted women the constitutional right to abortion. Nearly half a century later she witnessed the reversal of this decision.

She also spoke out in favour of the legalisation of same-sex marriage, as well as equal rights and pay for women, and protested against the death penalty and female genital mutilation.

Born on 25 March 1934 in Toledo, Ohio, she had a difficult childhood and did not go to school full-time until she was 12 years old.

After university in the late 1950s, she went to India on a research scholarship and spent two years in a variety of roles, including helping village women organise non-violent protests against government policies, which sparked her interest in grassroots activism.

She then moved to New York City in the early 1960s to start her career as a freelance writer. Her big break came through an exposé of Playboy Bunny working conditions.

Eventually she became a columnist for New York Magazine, before founding Ms. magazine in 1972.

Famously eschewing marriage, she went on to tie the knot in 2000 to David Bale, a South African-born entrepreneur-environmentalist and father of actor Christian Bale. He died three years later from brain lymphoma.

In 2013, then-President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honour in the US.

Her foundation said "she continued working for equality until the very end".

"Gloria's greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humour."

Her foundation said she lived her last years being in community and writing - welcoming guests into her home for "Talking Circles" - a tradition that will continue.

Her commitment to her home becoming a centre for social justice movements, and a forthcoming book An Unexpected Life, are "among many gifts Gloria has given the world with the hope they have ripple effects for generations to come", the foundation said.

Tributes flowed on Thursday after the news of her death, with writers and feminists commenting on Instagram with gratitude, some of them saying she had changed their lives.

Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and 2016 presidential candidate said Steinem was "one of the architects of the entire structure of women's equality, I mean tearing down those obstacles to young women being able to participate where their talents and hard work took them".

"Gloria was at heart an optimist," Clinton told CBS Mornings on Thursday.

"Her activism was rooted in optimism, and that's a moral choice, and she made it every day."

articles.title: In 1935, Melanchthon Cliser refused $4,855 for his 46-acre Virginia property; deputies handcuffed and evicted him, and he never cashed it as Shenandoah National Park took shape
articles.summary: US News: In 1935, Melanchton Cliser and his family were forced out of their 46-acre property in Virginia as the state pushed ahead with plans for what would be.
articles.body: In 1935, Melanchton Cliser and his family were forced out of their 46-acre property in Virginia as the state pushed ahead with plans for what would become Shenandoah National Park. Cliser owned the land along US 211 and also operated a gas station there. When he refused to leave, the local sheriff and his deputies came to remove him and his family.According to Virginia Center for Digital History, the deputies handcuffed Cliser, took the family's belongings out of their home and then sealed the house. The forced eviction was part of a much larger and difficult process in which hundreds of families were removed from land that was being acquired for the future national park.The creation of Shenandoah National Park had been discussed for years. Blue Ridge Mountains offered a scenic location for a national park that would be easily accessible to millions of people living in eastern US cities. The park was also expected to bring economic benefits to Virginia through tourism.But turning the plan into reality meant acquiring thousands of individual pieces of land. Many people living in the mountains did not want to leave their homes. The conflict became especially serious after the federal government made it clear that residents would have to leave before it would accept the land from Virginia.How park took shapeThe idea of creating a national park in Virginia gained serious attention in the 1920s. In 1924, Secretary of the Interior Hubert Work appointed the Southern Appalachian National Park Committee to study possible locations for a national park south of Pennsylvania.The committee visited the Blue Ridge and later recommended the area between Front Royal and Waynesboro. In 1926, Congress authorised the creation of a 521,000-acre Shenandoah National Park. However, the federal government could not use federal money to buy the land. Virginia and private groups had to raise the money needed for the purchases.The task proved much as thousands of separate tracts were involved, and many landowners did not have clear titles or agreed boundaries for their properties.William E Carson, head of Virginia's Commission on Conservation and Development, believed buying the land individually would take too long. He therefore pushed for a blanket condemnation law that would allow the state to acquire the required land through eminent domain.The state legislature passed the Public Park Condemnation Act in 1928. It allowed the state to file one condemnation case in each of the eight counties involved and created a Board of Appraisal Commissioners to determine the value of individual properties.Residents told to leaveThe process of acquiring land became closely linked to the question of what should happen to the people already living there. Several options were considerd including allowing residents to remain after selling their land, moving some families while allowing others to stay, or requiring everyone to leave.The idea that mountain residents were an obstacle to the park became increasingly influential. National Park Service official Arno Cammerer, on February 1, 1934, announced that the federal government would not accept land for the park until all residents had left the area.Resistance followed because many residents wanted to remain in their homes. Some had already moved voluntarily, but many others did not want to leave. Landowners also objected to the value assigned to their properties.The state eventually paid an average of about $12.50 per acre, but payments differed greatly. Some owners received as much as $131 per acre, while others received as little as $1 per acre. Many believed their land had been valued according to its agricultural potential rather than what it would be worth as part of the park.For residents such as Cliser, the dispute was about more than money. Some simply did not want to leave the homes and communities where they had lived.Forced evictions Landowners challenged the removal process in different ways. Some appealed property valuations, while others organised against the state's actions or appealed directly to political leaders.In 1933, H M Cliser of Beahm wrote to Governor Pollard, "I am relying wholly on the Constitution in this matter; therefore have nothing to arbitrate."The resistance sometimes resulted in direct confrontations. In October 1935, Melanchton Cliser and his family were among those who were forcibly removed.The sheriff and his deputies arrived at the family's home along US 211. When he continued to resist leaving, officers handcuffed him, removed the family's belongings and sealed the house. Cliser was reportedly offered $4,855 for his property but he never cashed the moneyThe park opens Despite the disputes, the park project moved forward. On December 26, 1935, the federal government accepted title to 176,429.8 acres from Virginia, exceeding the 160,000-acre minimum needed for the park to be established.On July 3, 1936, President Franklin Roosevelt and thousands of others attended the official dedication ceremony at Big Meadows. About 300 families were still living inside the park at that time. By early 1938, between 500 and 600 families had permanently left their homes in the park.Not everyone was forced to leave. In 1934, the park service secretly identified 43 families of 'aged and especially meritorious' people who were allowed to remain on their land rent-free after selling their property to the state.For most families, however, leaving the mountains marked the end of their lives there. The park service also began removing many signs of previous settlement by burning and tearing down structures.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Sure aims to 'minimise disruption' during 5G rollout in islands
articles.summary: Work is being done to minimise issues reported during a multimillion-pound network upgrade.
articles.body:
A telecom company says it aims to minimise disruption for customers as it continues to roll out its 5G network.

Sure is investing £48m in the upgrade across Guernsey and Jersey, with hopes to bring higher data speeds and better coverage to islanders.

CEO Alistair Beak said the "ambitious plan" was "a big complex programme", which had caused a minority of customers "some minor temporary disruptions".

He said the company aimed to minimise such issues and complete the rollout "in the next few months".

At the time a spokesperson said the issues experienced did "not all have one single cause" and individual customer cases were being investigated.

They advised people experiencing problems to contact the firm with details of the location, time and description of the problem.

Beak said the company had "put a lot of work into planning" and understanding "how the different technologies and the new network was going to work" alongside "what will become the old network".

He said: "By and large, it's working as we predicted.

"The vast majority of our customers are still making thousands of calls, are still using huge amounts of data and staying online and staying connected."

Beak said mobile coverage on the islands was expected to improve by up to 30% once the rollout was complete later this year.

articles.title: Disgraced ex-Reform Wales leader who took pro-Russian bribes must pay £22k
articles.summary: Nathan Gill was previously sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison last year for taking the bribes.
articles.body:
The former leader of Reform UK in Wales has been ordered to pay more than £22,500 after accepting bribes to make pro-Russian speeches in the European Parliament.

Gill, 53, of Llangefni on Anglesey, was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison in November 2025 after pleading guilty to eight counts of bribery under the Bribery Act 2010.

He is thought to have received up to £40,000 to help pro-Russian politicians in Ukraine, while he was a Member of the European Parliament (MEP).

At the Old Bailey on Thursday he was given six months to sell a rental property to pay the money to the UK government, or face a further nine months in prison.

Former Welsh Reform leader jailed for pro-Russia bribery

How WhatsApp messages revealed Gill's pro-Russian bribes

While a Member of the European Parliament (MEP) Gill had accepted money from Oleg Voloshyn, 44, a man once described by the US government as a "pawn" of Russian secret services.

Voloshyn was acting on behalf of a "close friend" of Vladimir Putin - Viktor Medvedchuk, 71, a former oligarch and pro-Russian Ukrainian politician who was the source of the requests and the cash.

In return for money, Gill gave speeches in the European Parliament and interviews to a now closed, pro-Russian TV channel in Ukraine.

He was the first British politician sentenced for the offence.

Gill did not appear at the short Old Bailey hearing this morning in which the UK government applied to confiscate £22,592.41.

Prosecuting Ben Holt told Judge Richard Marks that the sum to be paid had been agreed between the parties.

Clare Ashcroft, representing Gill, told the court that he would need time to sell his rental property to make the payment.

She said: "The property needs to be sold. Notice has been given to the tenants. Until these tenants vacate, that property cannot be put on the market."

It is understood the rental property is on Anglesey, the Press Association reported.

After hearing from defence counsel, Judge Richard Marks granted Gill six months in which to pay or face an extra term of nine months in prison.

Gill was an MEP from 2014 to 2020 - initially for UKIP and then the Brexit Party. He had briefly been a member of the Senedd - Wales' parliament - from 2016 to 2017, and had also served as UKIP's Welsh leader.

He led Reform UK's 2021 Welsh Parliament election campaign, but failed to be re-elected. He is no longer a member of the party.

In return for money he gave two TV interviews to 112 Ukraine in support for Medvedchuk, who had faced treason proceedings at the time.

The oligarch was detained by Ukrainian authorities at the start of the 2022 Russian full-scale invasion, and was later swapped with Moscow in a prisoner exchange.

Medvedchuk had been connected to two TV channels - 112 and NewsOne - which in 2018 and 2019 were under threat of closure by the Ukrainian authorities.

Gill gave two speeches defending the channels in the European Parliament, both on request from Voloshyn, whose wife was a presenter on 112 Ukraine.

Voloshyn also tasked Gill with finding other MEPs to speak to 112, and gave him talking points to pass on to them.

At the Old Bailey last year, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb said Gill had abused his position and had eroded "public confidence in democracy".

Reform UK said last year that the party had been glad justice had been served, calling his actions "reprehensible, treasonous and unforgivable".

The then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, accused Gill of "undermining our interests as a country".
